en: *Daodi jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Path), one fascicle.
Composed by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃgharakṣa (translated as Zhònghù in Chinese) of the Sūlāna country in India;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Parthian kingdom during the Later Han dynasty.

Chapter One: On the Scattering of Seeds From the appearance of the Victorious Sun, the semblance [of the Dharma] likewise manifests in color and conduct. Among those of great virtue, there are many who are most noble; their lineage is honored, and they maintain virtue through their conduct. It is from this seed that they arise, both in the world and in the heavens. All join their palms in homage to the Buddha; therefore, they pay obeisance by bowing their heads to the ground.
The Buddha is unsurpassed; there is none in the world whose diligence is equal to his. Ghosts, dragons, devas, and humans likewise follow him within the triple world.

He upholds the subtle and wondrous; those who have not crossed over, he causes to cross; the dead are no longer subject to death, and the aged are no longer subject to aging—all obtain the Buddha-dharma through following his practice.
Furthermore, this practice is the threefold absence of practice, which is also the guarding of virtue.
It is said that the Dharma of the Truths is produced from within one's own mind; when the practitioner attains its flavor, it is like pressing sugarcane. One must constantly observe with fear.
Even after accumulating more than a hundred years, if one does not attain the joy of the fruit, one will exhaust oneself through old age and death, and thus perish within the world.
For example, it is like a weak elephant that has fallen into a pit and cannot extricate itself.
People of the world are likewise; they derive comfort from various kinds of scriptures.
It is like a heap of various flowers placed upon the ground where one practices the path while remaining attached to the objects of desire.
If one wishes to hear the discourse on transcending the world, the practitioner shall listen; I shall now speak of the stages of practicing the Path.
Whether it be birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, grief, that which is disagreeable, or distress;
whether the practitioner practices while remaining at home or having renounced the home life—[all these shall be explained].
One who wishes to destroy the root of suffering and desires to attain the Way has no other refuge, no other resort, and no other means of liberation or dwelling; one must relinquish everything.
A practitioner such as this should simply practice total relinquishment, allowing the stages of the Path to follow from behind.

When one speaks of being attached to birth, old age, sickness, and death, or of the mental distress that gives rise to physical suffering, those who wish to transcend the world should then cultivate the stages of the Path and must not feel aversion toward the body.

Since old age, illness, and death already exist, if one gives rise to affliction by becoming attached to them, yet desires to follow and receive the Buddha’s precepts, one must then practice so as to reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is it that should not be practiced?
What is that which is to be practiced? What is the practitioner?
And what is the ground?

That which is not to be practiced consists of: mindfulness of desire, mindfulness of ill-will, mindfulness of harm, and mindfulness of one's country rather than mindfulness of death; following evil associates; not upholding the precepts, not receiving wisdom, not restraining the mind, not accepting instruction, and acting without inquiry;
and regarding one's own body as a source of mindfulness, perceiving it as form, and constantly delighting in the perception of purity;
reckoning for oneself that the body lacks wisdom, and dwelling in commanderies and counties among the weak and the common folk.
One’s mindfulness of forms is dim and hazy, not free from craving;
there is much desire, much ill-will, much delusion, many causal conditions, and much eating;

there is the practice of equanimity, attachment to bodily desires, drowsiness, forgetfulness of mind, and the fault of doubt; there is diligence that loses its vigor, fearfulness and failure to restrain the sense faculties, many affairs, much talk, many undertakings, and much busywork.
For a long time, the teaching has been inverted and intentions have been perverted.
It is just like this: when the phenomena of the present life follow what is not the Path or deviate from the Path, this is called "that which should not be practiced.
Why is it that this should not be practiced?

Because they are free from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and speaking in terms of subsequent bondage and constraint: harboring malice and the desire to kill, constantly perceiving the body as pleasant and pure, failing to follow with wisdom, and following after various evils—these, the Buddha says, are practices that should not be undertaken.
What is that which is to be practiced?
It is mindfulness of renunciation, not being mindful of ill will, not being mindful of killing, associating with wise friends, maintaining pure precepts, and moderation in eating;
it is examining oneself to avoid thoughts of what is wrong and to avoid thoughts of what is unwholesome.
One should contemplate suffering and contemplate impurity, not contemplating the excellence of the body;
one should not dwell in commanderies or counties, nor live among the weak;
one should not be dull-witted.
One maintains self-restraint, being free from affliction, free from busywork, and moderate in eating;
one does not abandon skillful means;
one subdues the body and relinquishes sleep, keeping the mind focused on right practice, guarding the mind so that it is free from doubt.
Diligence lies in practice: remaining free from alarm and fear while guarding the gates of the senses;

few words regarding the truths, practicing the reception of the teachings on the truths and cultivating the intention for the truths; delighting in empty marshes, practicing with contemplation as it truly is.
Before attaining the Good Dharma, one should strive to attain it; once attained, one should protect it.
One should take great joy in hearing the sutras, for while the physical body is sufficient for its needs, it is insufficient for the Dharma.

Knowing that death is certain, one should not delight in worldly virtues but grow weary of food and incline toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Those who practice the Dharma in this manner shall accordingly attain the unconditioned.
This is called that which is to be practiced.
Why is this to be practiced? Because from it one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

because from it one speaks of the purity of the precepts following subsequent constraints; because one falls into faith and does not dwell on the body; and because one collects and receives the affairs of the Dharma.
The listener perceives with clarity and does not transgress in any way; this accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

One who has attained the Way—when the Buddha preaches the Dharma—contemplates various kinds of mental states; there is neither suffering nor exhaustion. Having already explained the mass of merits, one should practice by restraining the faculties and subduing the body.
With what intention does the practitioner practice in accordance with the appropriate conduct?
The practitioner practices; the practitioner practices closely; this is called the practice of the practitioner.
There are three grades of such practitioners:
There are those who have not yet attained the Way: the learner and the non-learner.
What is the ground of the Way?
That which the practitioner practices is the ground of the practitioner.
What is the path for those who have not yet attained it?
It is the sequence of practices that originally arose; what was previously described constitutes this path.
Having thus concluded the explanation, both the learner and the non-learner have been discussed.
The stages of the Path of Practice (mārga-caryā-bhūmi) are termed "cessation and contemplation" (śamatha-vipaśyanā). What is the purpose of this cessation and contemplation?
It is simply because one has not yet attained the four virtues; therefore, one desires to bring these four virtues to realization.
Why should one seek to attain these four virtues?
It is because one seeks to attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through them.
By what causes and conditions is the unconditioned attained?
It is because one does not desire anything further.
Why does one not desire anything further?
It is solely because one desires to eliminate all suffering.
Therefore, a practitioner who wishes to eliminate all suffering should never depart from, violate, or pierce the established practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
If a practitioner pierces [this practice], they will obtain neither *śamatha* nor *vipaśyanā*, and their ascetic practice will be empty and lost.

It is like a person seeking fire who drills wood; he drills the upper piece against the lower piece, but stops from time to time and pauses his drilling from time to time. In this way, he never obtains fire and only exhausts himself with toil.
The Path is like this, as explained from the subsequent perspective:

Suppose that while practicing the contemplation of dharmas, one becomes weary and disenchanted; the practitioner should then set aside the practice, neither piercing nor exhausting oneself. If one who is weary continues the practice, they will lose the Way.
It is like a person walking in the deepest darkness at night with their eyes closed; when will they ever see the light? If a practitioner’s practice is unbroken, the wise are likewise:

as the sun rises and they walk with eyes open, their wisdom gradually increases. Such a person attains the seeds of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). While some who have mastered the sūtras may simply recite them, those who have further mastered the sūtras contemplate the scriptural teachings and then explain *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whereas other sūtras provide only scattered explanations.
This concludes the chapter on the Scattering of Seeds in the Stages of the Path (*Bhūmi*). 2.

The Chapter on Knowing the Wisdom of the Five Aggregates (*Pañcaskandha-prajñā*), the Second Chapter of the *Sūtra on the Stages of the Path*. One attains firm clarity through various sūtras; it is the nectar of non-aging and non-death. One’s fame and renown spread through practice like the bright moon. For the practitioner, the pure one, and the one of luminous wisdom, if they maintain the precepts, they become even more radiant; this is likewise true for those who act within the household!
Evil intent cannot be grasped, nor can it be led according to one's whims.

Therefore, one who bestows gifts upon those who have attained the Way and pays homage to those who have attained the Way bows their head because they follow that which has attained the nectar of immortality.
Greed is the seed; because it is abundant, it gives rise [to further existence]. The joy and delight of craving constitute the factor of sorrow.
The Buddha taught that the five aggregates are like a lute; one should listen to and study many sūtras to lead practitioners along the path.

One should know that the body is fundamentally composed of five elements: the element of form, the element of sensation, the element of perception, the element of mental formations, and the element of consciousness.

Just as there are various districts in the east, various districts in the south, various districts in the west, and various districts in the north, yet a single house is not called a district; so it is with these five elements.
This analogy for form is such that neither a single form constitutes the category of form, nor do various forms constitute the category of form;
it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Form resides within the ten bases; as for the texts, they also follow from the Dharma. The base of sensation is the category of form; the one hundred and eight feelings are the category of feeling; the one hundred and eight perceptions are the category of perception; the one hundred and eight formations are the category of formations; the one hundred and eight consciousnesses are the category of consciousness. Thus, one should know that these five categories manifest from the latter.
This parable speaks of things that are not interconnected, yet it is solely due to fundamental ignorance;
because one has not heard the Buddha’s words, or because one is habituated to delusion.
For example, just as tree leaves adhere to branches, so do delusion and evil conduct adhere to the five aggregates, forming a mass of these five, which the mind conceptualizes as "this body."
Chapter Three: On the Endowment of Appropriate Characteristics, from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (The Section on the Wisdom of the Five Aggregates within the Stages of the Path).

In this chapter on the endowment of appropriate characteristics, the river of nature flows open and fills the vessels of those to be saved; it shatters the six pādas of the *Śrāvaka-piṭaka* like honey, and suddenly, as a lotus blooms and the sun of wisdom rises, one partakes of the supreme lotus and serves the Buddha. Thus, its characteristics are pure, serene, and tranquil.
The Most Honored One, whose blessings and protection are peerless in the world, beholding their essential firmness and intending to guide them, expounded it according to the Sūtras.

Having already transformed and guided those who practice the Way, one should also know the five kinds of characteristics that correspond to each other: the characteristic of the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) is form, the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*) is also form, and the hand holding the lute is also form;
furthermore, sensation (*vedanā*) is the characteristic of sensation—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful sensations—this is the characteristic of sensation.
The characteristic of consciousness is volition; whether it pertains to a woman, a man, or others, this is the characteristic of volition.
What is performed is action (*saṃskāra*); whether it is wholesome action, unwholesome action, neither wholesome nor unwholesome action, this is the characteristic of action.
The characteristic of consciousness is consciousness itself; whether it is pleasant, unpleasant, or neither unpleasant nor pleasant, this is the characteristic of consciousness.
These five types each have their own characteristics.

Speaking from the latter perspective, it is said that even within this form there are many evils; as the Buddha taught in the sūtras, these should be expounded accordingly, describing the various characteristics and aspects of the five aggregates as they correspond to their respective natures.
Chapter Four: The Analysis and Manifestation of the Cessation of the Five Aggregates within the Stages of the Path (Mārgabhūmi).

The fifth section: The Analysis and Manifestation of the Cessation of the Five Aggregates. One takes up the seeds of ambrosia to drench the five aggregates of clinging; using the five aggregates as fuel, one employs the light of wisdom to extinguish the fire of evil.

I pay homage to you, who receive the salutations of those from the three realms; you who uphold the nectar that extinguishes the three poisons; you who emerge from the drill of the five aggregates as appropriate; you who uphold the mind of wisdom to extinguish the fire of the evil mind; you who are honored within the three realms—I too honor you with palms joined in reverence.
Since the power of wisdom has been attained by the wise through their own realization, just as they have known it for themselves, the Buddha has taught his disciples that which should be practiced.

Hearing and understanding this, one’s mind becomes concentrated; through the discernment of the five aggregates, that which is guarded by the power of wisdom is known as the purity of the Buddha himself. When that which is known according to one’s intention manifests as actual reality, this is what the Buddha taught as the practice to be undertaken and the vision to be realized.
It is said that one discerns the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) through this concentration.
A practitioner on the path should know how to discern the five aggregates.
How, then, should the practitioner discern and know the five aggregates?

For example, suppose a string of pearls were dropped at a crossroads. One person sees it; having seen it, they feel affection for it, their mind delights in it, and they desire to obtain the pearls. Their intent being fixed upon the pearls, this constitutes the seed of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
That which is pleasing and agreeable to the mind constitutes the seed of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).
If, as described above, one regards the string itself as the "string of pearls," this constitutes the seed of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).
If the mind gives rise to desire and grasps the beads on the string, this constitutes the seed of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
from this knowledge arises the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Thus, these five types [of seeds] reside upon a single string and proceed together; they perform various activities and also proceed spontaneously. Just as they proceed simultaneously upon a single string, so too do the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) function in this manner.

Regarding the forms seen by the eye and the five modes of conduct that accompany them, as well as sounds heard by the ear, fragrances smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the mouth, and the coarse or subtle sensations felt by the body—within these bodily aggregates, there is no production of the seed of form; thus, one should discern and know each of these seeds of the five aggregates individually.

Later, there were those who spoke of the Way and its virtue; having analyzed and explained it in this manner, they obtained the teaching of this sutra. Those who had not yet attained the Way accepted and clung to it with their minds, and with such mental activity they spoke, saying, "I too now proclaim this teaching."
Chapter on the Manifestation of the Cessation through the Analysis of the Five Aggregates in the Practice of the Path.

Chapter Five: The Fivefold Success and Failure. In the *Dàodì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Path), Chapter Five: The Fivefold Success and Failure: One already knows that attaining Buddhahood is essential; the essentials are completed, the essentials are performed, the essentials are attained together, and the essentials are finished together. Once the essentials are fulfilled, there are no further essentials to be pursued. One should pay homage to the Unattached One, whose fame is immeasurable and whose spoken words are authoritative.

Just as the bright moon brings clear knowledge to its disciples, so too does one who fears the offenses arising from the mind and is able to destroy their roots gain clarity regarding the five aggregates; knowing that their formation and disintegration are like a dream, you should bow your head and listen.
The Buddha said:
"One who practices the Way should know the arising and ceasing, the emergence and entry, of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

It is like when a person's life is about to end and remains only in their breath; as they are on the verge of death, the four hundred and four diseases gradually manifest in succession from beginning to end."
Then he perceives the arising of thoughts of fear and dread; in his dreams he sees bees pecking at wood, and crows and vultures pecking at the crown of his head.
Upon a single-pillar tower he sees himself joyfully dressed in garments—blue, yellow, red, and white—worn upon his own body; he sees horsemen riding and herds of cattle lowing.
They used their alms bowls as pillows and slept upon heaps of earth.
They carried the dead, served as scavengers for latrines, and ate from the same vessel;
they were seen traveling together in carts, with their feet and bodies smeared with sesame oil and mud.
He also sees himself drinking at various times;
he also sees himself fallen into a net and led away by hunters;
or he sees himself laughing, rejoicing, and exulting.
Or one may see a pile of tadpoles passing over oneself;
or see salt-money being gathered;
or see a woman with disheveled hair and bared body, pulling oneself along by the hand.
Some have ashes smeared on their bodies and also eat;
some see dogs and monkeys chasing one another in fear;
or they see themselves dying, yet seeking to marry.
At times he sees the household deities in people's homes being destroyed;
at times he sees horses licking his beard and hair;
at times he sees his teeth falling to the ground.
At times he sees himself wearing the clothes of a dead person;
at times his own body is naked and smeared with oil;
or he sees himself rolling upon a heap of earth.
At times he saw people wearing leather and woolen garments walking about;
at other times he saw the gate of his own house, where a dilapidated carriage arrived, laden with oil, flowers, and incense.
He also sees his brothers close to himself, and the ancestors appearing with coarse and terrifying countenances, wishing to come and seize him to go along with them.
At times he walks among the tombs, suddenly casting away flower garlands from around his neck;
at other times he sees himself falling headlong into the waters of a river.
At times they see themselves falling into the five lakes and nine rivers, unable to reach the bottom;
at times they see themselves entering among the reeds and thatch, naked, cutting one another, and rolling about upon what they have spread out;
at times they climb trees that bear no fruit, no flowers, and no blossoming playthings.
At times he danced upon the altar;
at times he wandered alone among the trees, finding great delight in them, and also split logs of various kinds of wood into firewood;
at times he entered a house and, being in the dark, could not find the door to exit.
At times he ascends steep, jagged mountains and weeps aloud in grief;
at times birds peck at his feet or even trample them;
at times dust covers his head.

At times, one may be blocked by tigers, or likewise by dogs, monkeys, or donkeys; traveling southward, one enters a cemetery and sees heaps of charcoal, hair, fur, scattered bones, and crushed stalks of flowers, while seeing oneself enter the realm of King Yama.
When the messenger of King Yama questioned him, he appeared from behind and spoke:

"The world has already experienced much pleasure; now, with the faculties failing or the body collapsing, you fear for your life and seek to depart, yet find no autonomy. Illness pursues you and hastens you on; the mind is already agitated. As life reaches its end and sorrow draws near, you shall see a dream that plunges you into great terror."
The person then thinks within their mind:
"My life is about to end; such was the dream seen by my body.
Thereupon, their mind becomes terrified and their body becomes withered.
It is like a bird that has stepped on a thorn; its body is pressed against it with extreme pain, and it wishes to seek refuge with a physician.
Its kinsmen and brothers, seeing the severity of its illness, dispatch a messenger to the physician’s house.

As soon as he called for his messengers to set out, these signs appeared: they were unclean and wore foul garments; their nails were long and their hair and beards disheveled; they rode a dilapidated and broken-down carriage and wore tattered sandals;
their complexions were dark and their eyes were blue; white oxen and horses drew the carriage, and they stroked their own hair and beards with their own hands.
Having summoned the physician, he hurriedly had him mount the carriage and bound him from behind.

Because his mind was solely intent on wicked pleasures, he paid no heed to wholesome joys nor considered illness and medicine; once his body was ruined, he fell into the vessel of transgression. He immediately sent for the physician, who then thought:
"The pain and illness will not allow him to recover."
Why is this? It is merely to make him appear to have such a likeness: his attire, speech, carriage, parasol, beard, hair, and clothing;

likewise, they summon him on memorial days—whether the fourth, sixth, ninth, twelfth, or fourteenth—and further, they encounter days that are taboo, which physicians dislike, as well as the "blood-taboo" (*xièjì*) and the "fourth-contrary" (*sìjī fǎnzhī*) days upon which he is summoned.
This also does not necessarily depend on the time, the hours, the watches, or the constellations.
To require such things for even a moment would be to suspect people of grasping at signs. Why is this so?

Sometimes, even when the day and the hour are unfavorable, there may be a person who employs skillful means and is able to cure illnesses; yet at other times, despite such efforts, the illness cannot be cured. Therefore, it does not necessarily depend upon the specific day or the specific hour.
Therefore, wise people do not take pleasure in calculating the days.
The *ṛṣis* constantly advise:

"One should seek skillful means for treatment; even until death, if one suffers from illness or sudden affliction, it may be possible to recover. However, if one's life has reached its end, simply say 'I am going.'"
It can be calculated that one may thus reach the house of illness, which is bound from behind;
it is said that they all enter the sea, where some arrive and some perish midway. Illness is likewise compared to the sea: some are cured, while others die.

The physician then proceeded to the house of the patient. Hearing sounds that were unpleasant to him—sounds of things being lost, burnt, severed, broken, pierced, pulled, scraped, brushed away, cast out, killed, departed, arisen, extinguished, or corroded—and seeing things burnt, severed, broken, pierced, pulled, scraped, brushed away, cast out, killed, departed, arisen, extinguished, or corroded beyond the point of treatment and already dead; he looked toward the south and again saw crows and ravens making noise in their nests;
he saw children together, throwing dust at one another;
and he saw naked men pulling each other’s hair and breaking jars, basins, tiles, and bowls.
He also saw empty houses and felt no attachment to them.
When he arrived at the house of the sick man and entered to see the afflicted person, he found the illness even more distressing.

As the physician looked upon the patient from that room, the latter was suddenly seized with terror; startled, he sat up, yet being stricken by the disease, he lacked strength and could not regain his composure.
Seeing this, he then reflects:

"In such a sutra, the signs of death are described: the complexion becomes inferior, the skin wrinkles, the body takes on the color of earth, the tongue protrudes, or speech is forgotten; one perceives the body as heavy and the joints as unresponsive; the tip of the nose becomes crooked, the skin turns black and withered, and the throat and tongue take on the color of bone, no longer perceiving flavors."

The mouth is parched and the pores are red; the sinews and veins are no longer distinct. With hair disheveled and standing on end, he pulls at his hair yet feels no sensation. He stares straight ahead while lying on his back; his expression turns to one of terror, his face wrinkles, and his hair stands erect as he gazes intently, sometimes uttering various words.
As the Sūtra says:
"The remaining life is not worth mentioning; it is like a fire breaking out among the trees, or like the six characteristics—there is nothing to be said regarding what is heard or seen.
It is like the fragrance of sandalwood when one has washed the body but before the body has been fully cleansed.
At times it is like the fragrance of honey;
at times it is the fragrance of many-seeded incense;
at times it is the fragrance of natika.
At times the fragrance of roots;
at times the fragrance of bark;
at times the fragrance of flowers.
At times it is the fragrance of melons;
at times the fragrance of *huo* incense;
at times the fragrance resulting from past habitual conduct, such as the fragrance of sinews, hair, bones, flesh, blood, or excrement.
Sometimes the fragrance of an owl;
sometimes the fragrance of a crow;
sometimes the fragrance of a viper.
At times it has the scent of a pig;
at times the scent of a dog;
at times the scent of a monkey.
At times it has the scent of a rat;
at times the scent of a snake;
and at times it is like that of a human being.
At times there is the sound of woodpeckers;
at times the sound of tiles;
at times a rasping sound.
At times there was the sound of harsh voices;
at times the sound of geese;
at times the sound of peacocks.
At times there was the sound of drums;
at times the sound of horses;
and at times the sound of tigers.

There is also another explanation regarding the signs of death as it reaches maturity: for example, when a person is dying, there are signs of death such as the mouth no longer perceiving flavors, the ears no longer hearing sounds, and the entire body contracting and shriveling. The veins sink into the flesh and blood; the jaw slackens and opens wide; the head shakes and droops without clarity; the buttock muscles stiffen; the eyes turn black; the large and small intestines become obstructed; the joints and roots loosen; and a bitter, greenish froth bubbles up from the mouth with double hiccups.

Such symptoms of illness and pain are incurable; even if one were to assemble all the skilled physicians, including the *bhringarāja* and the *śatapatra*, along with every kind of sacrificial rite, they would still be unable to cure it.
Then the physician thought to himself, "This patient's illness is such that his life is at its end; I ought to avoid him.
He then said to the members of his household:

"Regarding this illness, do not think of what he desires; let him have whatever he wishes and do not restrain him. There is a small matter in my household that must be settled, after which I shall depart.
He spoke these words in private to the patient’s family members:
"He can no longer be cured."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
When the family of the sick person heard the physician’s words, they immediately discarded the medicine and ceased all the medical treatments they had been performing.

Relatives, friends, and neighbors gathered together and crowded around the suffering patient, weeping and gazing upon him with grief. It was like a herd of cattle when one is being slaughtered by a butcher; seeing the dead cow, the remaining cattle fear that they themselves will meet the same fate, leaping about the pen in terror and fleeing into the mountains and trees while crying out.
Furthermore, it is like a pig being slaughtered by a butcher; when the other pigs see this, they are struck with terror and fear, feigning death, and pricking up their ears to stare straight ahead.

It is also like fish that have fallen into a net for the sake of a fisherman; when the other fish see this, they are terrified and dive away, fleeing into the sand and stones or hiding among the water-weeds.
Again, it is like a flock of flying birds; if one bird is caught by a hawk or a falcon, the other birds are startled and scatter in all directions.

Thus, brothers, kinsmen, acquaintances, and neighbors see them with pity at their departure; they watch as their lives are about to be severed, and the messengers of hell have already arrived to lead them into prison. Having died right there, once the arrow has been shot and the noose of birth-and-death has cast its line, their transgressions drag them away into the world beyond.

When the relatives have returned and gathered up his disheveled hair and beard, if he continues to utter cries of anguish that fill his mouth and do not cease, speaking words of sorrow that reveal his deep affection, shedding various kinds of tears and spittle from his chin, and crying out, "What shall we do!"?
"The patient will not survive much longer. Within him arises a wind named 'Sword-Wind,' which causes the joints of the patient to disperse;
another wind arises named 'Hasty-Wind,' which causes the ligaments of the patient to snap;
yet another wind arises named 'Needle-Wind,' which causes the tendons of the patient to slacken."
Furthermore, there is one wind named Asthi-bheda-vāyu (the bone-breaking wind), which causes the marrow of the patient to be injured.

Furthermore, there is one wind named Koṣṭha-vāyu (the visceral wind), which causes the eyes, ears, and nasal orifices of the patient to turn entirely blue, and causes all the hair of the head and body to emerge from these orifices, breaking, severing, and pulling them out.

Furthermore, there is one wind named Urdhva-ga-vāyu (the upward-moving wind), which causes the internal parts of the patient—the knees, flanks, shoulders, back, chest, abdomen, navel, lower abdomen, large intestine, small intestine, liver, lungs, heart, spleen, kidneys, and other viscera—to be severed and cut asunder.

Furthermore, there is another wind called the "Forming Wind" (*abhinirvartaka-vāyu*), which causes the patient's blood and adipose tissue to turn blue, and produces disorders of feces and urine, as well as heat, cold, and astringency in both the digested and undigested portions; it also causes the limbs to retract from their positions.

Furthermore, there is another wind called the "Wind Residing in the Joints" (*sandhi-sthita-vāyu*), which causes the patient's bones and joints to become stiff and convulse, or at times causes them to lift their hands and feet, grasp at empty space, stand up, sit down, groan, weep, or become enraged.

The joints have already been dispersed, the fetters have already been severed, the sinews have already slackened, and the marrow has already been wounded. Vitality and clarity have departed together; only the physical frame remains. The mind has grown cold like wood; it has abandoned the five aggregates, and within the heart there is only a faint, lingering trace of existence.

It is like the residual light remaining after a lamp has been extinguished; when the mind is withdrawn, there remains only a subtle consciousness. This consciousness perceives the good and evil, the merits and demerits, that a person has habitually practiced, and the mind then beholds them.
In this present life, if one habitually practices what is wholesome, the mind rejoices; if one commits what is unwholesome, one immediately feels shame.
Those who attain a favorable rebirth find joy in their minds, while those who fall into an unfavorable rebirth feel sorrow and shame.

It is like a person looking into a clear mirror who sees his entire reflection: the graying hair, the wrinkled skin, the impurities and dust upon his body, the falling teeth, or the stained teeth; seeing his body thus subject to old age, he repeatedly feels such shame that he closes his eyes and puts away the mirror, unwilling to look. Because of the sorrow caused by putting away the mirror, he thinks: "My vigor has departed; old age has arrived; my complexion is ugly; my pleasures have gone."
Thus, having habitually practiced evil and followed evil conduct with one's own mind, one then experiences sorrow, regret, suffering, and unpleasantness, reproaching oneself:
"Now there is no doubt that I have fallen into an evil state."

"If a practitioner practices the three types of excellence and maintains various vows of conduct, and if that most excellent practitioner possesses much goodness, they should immediately feel great joy and a joyful mind, thinking to themselves:
'I have now ascended to heaven and am in a most excellent state.'"
"It is like a merchant who, having escaped a perilous path, gains great profit and rejoices upon returning home and reaching his door;
it is also like a farmer’s wish fulfilled when he harvests the five grains and stores them in his house;
and it is like one suffering from illness who attains healing and peace."
It is also like having repaid a debt;
one's natural conduct is likewise in harmony with virtuous practice.
It is like a honeybee that thinks to itself, "I have reached a favorable place."

"At that moment, the physical body and consciousness cease, and immediately there is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). It is like a scale rising on one side while falling on the other; in this way, one abandons death and takes up the seed of birth. It is like planting grain: once the root has sprouted, the stalk grows forth."

In this same way, at the time of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as consciousness ceases, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise immediately; they are complete and not deficient. Nor do the aggregates of death transmigrate to obtain the aggregates of the intermediate state, nor are they separate from the aggregates of death, for there are the aggregates of the intermediate state.
There are only the five aggregates of death, yet from them the five aggregates of the intermediate state arise.

It is like a person holding a seal and pressing it onto soft clay; within the clay there then appears the impression of the seal. The seal does not travel to the clay, nor does the clay depart from the image of the seal.
For example, it is like the root of a seed: the seed is not the root, yet the root is not separate from the seed.

The human spirit (*pudgala*) is also like this: according to its smallness or greatness as prescribed by the Dharma, it proceeds from birth to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and from that intermediate state it comes into existence.

"Among those who practice well, one obtains the five aggregates (skandhas) of excellence; among those who practice evil, one obtains the aggregates of evil. For those who obtain the aggregates, there is the practice of the divine eye (divyacakṣus); for those who abide in the intermediate state, there are three sustenances:
pleasure, mindfulness, and consciousness."
As for those who cease [the process of rebirth], they may remain for one day or up to seven days; when they reach the assembly of their parents, they also cease from wherever they were falling.

When they are about to die at the place where they were falling, having already produced the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), they immediately give rise to a thousand thoughts, or upon seeing and recollecting [the parents], delusion arises.
"Those who have committed the most heinous deeds naturally find themselves at the edge of a great fire;
there, hundreds of thousands of crows, ravens, hawks, and falcons gather together.

They also see people with hideous claws, faces, teeth, and garments, their heads aflame, as they administer various poisons from their hands. Seeing from afar a thicket of trees, the thought arises to enter within; thus the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) ceases, and one is born in that place of descent. Immediately thereafter, before long, one sees the Sword-Leaf Trees (*asipattravana*) and falls into them—this is called hell."
"The arising of the five aggregates and the six sense bases are sinful and are all evil practices; immediately one sees fierce smoke, dust, fire, wind, and rain falling upon the body.
Furthermore, one sees elephants, lions, tigers, and vipers, fearing for one's own life.
One also sees a mountain well that closes up behind one, and one comes to a halt at a precipitous cliff."

When the intention enters [the new state], one immediately abandons the intermediate state body; once the mind-born [existence] has arisen, the intermediate state ceases and one falls into birth, arriving before long in the animal realm.

Later, manifesting extreme delusion and lacking propriety, they harbor evil intentions toward their parents; they constantly delight in coarse speech, anger, binding, beating, and committing evil deeds. Such a person who takes what is not given shall fall among the animals.

"When one's offenses are lightened, a scorching wind arises; life is tormented by hunger and the body is encircled by knives, spears, and drills. Returning humans also see great pits, and their minds arise with the thought that they shall enter them."

This is precisely the mind-born [being]; it then extinguishes the intermediate state (antarābhava) and receives the aggregates (skandha) of the place where it is to fall, immediately falling into the realm of hungry ghosts (preta). Thus, such a falling is called "falling as a hungry ghost."

Following the practice of those who hold such views, two base and wicked thieves converse together, slandering, violating precepts, and engaging in false and delusive discourse. They consume all manner of food without avoiding what is evil or impure; though they follow the good, they do not practice the Dharma. Consequently, they fall into the mire of blood-oaths and spittle—this is called falling into the realm of hungry ghosts.

"Those who practice what is best obtain the most excellent bliss; they are also fanned by fragrant breezes, as various kinds of flowers scatter upon their bodies, various kinds of musical sounds accompany them, and various kinds of trees stand within their gardens."

As soon as the mind arises, it enters; at that moment, once the mind has arisen, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) ceases, and one undergoes birth in the aggregates to which one is destined. Thus, one immediately receives a celestial body.

In this way, one falls into the heavens; those who have performed meritorious deeds fall into the heavens to which they correspond, and having already not departed from these dharmas, this constitutes the seed of falling into the heavens.

"If one falls among humans, one receives calamities or blessings according to one's original conduct; parents likewise gather together, and through the correspondence of past deeds, one is born as a male, with fortune remaining equal [to that of the parents]."
At that time, the parents' vital essence is gathered, yet the womb-entrance (*garbhadvāra*) is not firm; it is neither affected by wind, heat, nor cold, nor is it stained or distorted;
it is neither too frequent nor too constricted;
it does not crave food, nor is it agitated, nor arrogant, nor does it destroy the womb-entrance.
It does not resemble a chestnut, nor a wheel;
it does not resemble a raccoon, nor barley;
its center does not resemble native steel, nor tin; and throughout all its gates, there is no malevolent spirit.
It is neither thin nor thick;
it is neither putrid nor black, neither red nor yellow, and its colors do not disperse.
It is not a mixture of wind, blood, cold, or heat, nor is it combined with urine and semen.

The spirit has already halted the vital essence (*śukra*). The spirit’s thought turns toward the intention to produce desire; it repels the male and takes its place within itself to experience pleasure with the weak man.

The weak man then hates his father and delights in his mother; having already delighted, his non-delight increases as the intention arises. He should then repel the male’s desire and experience pleasure alone with the weak man; he then immediately establishes himself at the gate of the womb (*garbhadvāra*), and once the intention has arisen, he repels the male.

When I was emaciated and performed prostrations, my parents immediately discharged their vital essence (*śukra*). The spirit (*manas*) then arrived and thought, "This is my essence. It was born through the power of its own volition; having been born through that joy, its traces were extinguished within that joy, and it was then produced from the semen and blood.

"Consciousness resides within the semen and further arises within craving; though the consciousness of craving does not fall into the semen, it nevertheless arises from the fundamental source as the consciousness of craving. The semen is the body of the child, and that which is craved arises within the semen—this is the seed of sensation (vedanā).
Once it is known to be semen, that which constitutes the semen is the fundamental source of the seed of volitional thought (saṃskāra);
the activity of mental attention is the seed of birth and death."
Knowing that semen is the seed of consciousness constitutes the five essential factors.
At that moment, one attains two faculties:
The body faculty and the mind faculty.
After seven days, the seminal essence has not yet diminished; after two weeks, the seminal essence is produced, thin like the cream on the surface of curdled milk;
after three weeks, the seminal essence coagulates, like thickened curd remaining in a vessel.
In the fourth week, the semen becomes somewhat solid, like curdled milk.
In the fifth week, the semen undergoes transformation, like butter made from curds.
In the sixth week, it is like butter, becoming a solid mass through transformation. In the seventh week, it is like butter, becoming a solid mass through transformation.
In the seventh seven-day period, the mass of transformations becomes a solid core, like well-cooked millet porridge.
In the eighth seven-day period, the transformations of the millet porridge cease, becoming like a ground pebble.
In the ninth week, while on the grindstone, five protuberances (*uṣṇīṣa*) arose:
the mark of the two shoulders, the mark of the two kneecaps, and the mark of the head.
In the seventeenth week, also while on the grindstone, four elbows arose.
The marks of the two hands and the marks of the two feet.
On the seventy-first day, he was also born upon the whetstone with twenty-four cubits:
ten on the marks of the fingers, ten on the marks of the toes, and four on the marks of the locations of the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth.
The twelfth seven-day period is correctly measured as one *zhǔ*.
In the thirteenth seven-day period, the signs of the abdomen’s emergence appear.
In the fourteenth seven-day period, the heart, spleen, kidneys, liver, and mind are produced.
In the fifteenth week, the large intestine is formed;
in the sixteenth week, the small intestine is formed;
in the seventeenth week, the stomach is formed.
In the eighteenth week, there are the places of the liver, the lungs, and the spleen.
In the nineteenth week, there are the thighs, knees, feet, arms, palms, joints, and the ankles of the hands and feet.
In the twenty-seventh week, the navel, the breasts, the neck, and the nape of the neck take shape.

In the twenty-first week, the marrow begins to form within the bones: nine bones are attached to the head, two to the cheeks, thirty-two to the mouth, seven to the throat, two to the shoulders, two to the upper arms, forty to the wrists, twelve to the knees, sixteen to the ribs, eighteen to the spine, two to the larynx, two to the hips, four to the shins, and fourteen to the feet; furthermore, one hundred and eight minute bones grow within the flesh.
Thus, three hundred joints emerge from the minute elements and attach to the body, resembling a gourd.
In the twenty-second week, the bones become somewhat firm, like the shell of a tortoise.
In the twenty-third week, the vital essence (śukra) becomes firm again, like a thick-shelled walnut.

These constitute three hundred joints connected to one another: the bones of the feet are connected to the calves; the calves are connected to the hip bones; the hip bones are connected to the back; the spinal and waist bones are connected to the shoulders; the shoulders are connected to the neck; the neck is connected to the head and jaw; and the head and jaw are connected to the teeth.

Thus, this is a heap of bones, a rugged city of bone, bound by sinews, drenched in blood, plastered with flesh, and covered by skin; from it one receives the fruits of merit, yet there is no sensation of pain or itching that is not known, as it moves according to the will and the winds, twitching and contorting.
In the twenty-fourth week, seven thousand sinews wrap around the body.
In the twenty-fifth week, seven thousand vessels are produced, though they are not yet fully formed.
In the twenty-sixth week, all the vessels are completely permeated and fully perfected, like the pores of a lotus root.
On the twenty-seventh week, the three hundred and sixty joints are fully formed.
On the twenty-eighth week, the sprouts of flesh arise.
On the twenty-ninth week, the flesh becomes somewhat firm and full.
On the thirty-seventh day, the membranes form a waxy layer.
On the thirty-first day, the membranes become somewhat firm.
On the thirty-second day, the buttocks and muscles begin to grow.
In the thirty-third week, the ears, nose, abdomen, spleen, and adipose tissue are formed and become discernible through medical examination.
In the thirty-fourth week, ninety-nine hundred thousand pores develop on the surface of the skin within the body.
In the thirty-fifth week, the nine million nine hundred thousand pores gradually become manifest.
In the thirty-sixth week, the nails grow.
In the thirty-seventh week, various winds arise within the mother’s womb; some winds arise that cause the eyes, nose, and mouth to open, and once opened, they enter [the air].
Furthermore, winds may arise that cause hair, body hair, nails, and teeth to grow—whether they are well-formed or not;

or winds may arise that alter the complexion of the flesh, making it white, black, yellow, or red, and whether it is beautiful or not. During these seven days, the brain, blood, fat, marrow, and spinal fluid undergo changes, and the channels for heat, cold, mucus, and the excretory passages open.
In the thirty-eighth week, a wind arises within the mother’s womb that causes [the fetus] to experience the good and evil deeds of its past lives:
if one has performed good deeds, a fragrant wind arises, making the body and mind upright and pleasing to others;

if one has performed evil deeds, a foul wind arises, causing the body and mind to be restless and unpleasing to others, with the bones and joints being misshapen—perhaps harelipped, or crooked, or hunchbacked, or dwarfed—so that people find them loathsome upon seeing them.
At thirty-eight weeks, which is nine months minus four days, the bones and joints are all fully formed.
Regarding the past karmic actions of the child at birth, there are two portions:
one portion is derived from the father, and one portion is derived from the mother.
At times, the hair, body hair, tongue, throat, navel, heart, liver, spleen, eyes, buttocks, and blood are derived from the mother;
while the nails, bones, marrow, feces, urine, vessels, semen, and other skeletal joints are derived from the father.
The karmic predispositions from past actions determine the descent into birth: those that have matured descend below, while those yet to ripen ascend above.
A male child remains at the left flank with his back toward the front and his abdomen toward the rear;
a female child remains at the right flank with her abdomen toward the front and her back toward the rear.
The place of rest is foul and filthy; all the bones and joints are curled and shriveled within a leather bag. Inside the belly, blood clings to the body, while outside, excrement grows fat and long.

"When there are four days remaining of the ninth month, during those first or second days, if one’s past conduct has been good, the thought arises: 'I am in a garden,' or one imagines: 'I am in the heavens';
if one’s conduct has been evil, the thought arises: 'I am staying in hell.'"
On the second day, the mind is focused on the third day; this is the pleasure within the womb.

On the third day, the mind is focused on the fourth day. For one day and one night, winds arise within the mother’s womb, moving upward and downward; by means of these winds, the child turns head-downward and feet-upward, falling into the mother’s birth canal.

Those whose past conduct was virtuous, when their consciousness descends into the mother’s womb, conceive the thought of entering a pool of water and playing therein; they may further conceive the thought of being upon a high couch or amidst fragrant flowers.

Those whose past conduct was evil, when their consciousness descends, conceive the thought of falling from a mountain onto a tree, onto a bank, into a pit, into a latrine, into thorns, into a net, into straw, or into a fence of swords and spears. Their descent proceeds with distress and haste, yet it may also proceed with joy, pleasure, or a sense of renown.
Bound by their own good and evil deeds, wherever they go, they find themselves subject to further suffering.

Once enveloped by the fetal membranes, squeezed through the narrow birth canal, and cast onto the ground where they encounter the winds, they are then washed with warm water by others. Their hands feel coarse against their bodies, which ache all over as if covered in sores; from this point on, they forget their past conduct and what they experienced within the womb.

Once born, because of the stench of blood, they immediately coalesce into malevolent ghosts, *ḍākinīs*, and *pīśācas*; each becomes a *kumbhāṇḍa*, practicing as a *gū*, *mārīci*, or *churicā*. It is the same for their fathers.
It is like a piece of meat at a crossroads, which vultures, hawks, crows, magpies, and various other birds vie for, each desiring to possess it;
they circle it and harass people in this manner.
If one’s past conduct was good, one cannot be afflicted;
if one’s past conduct was evil, one can be afflicted.
Not long after birth, the mother nourishes it with milk; as it gradually grows larger, it begins to eat and drink. Once it is able to eat and drink, eighty kinds of worms arise within its body.
Two types arise from the roots of the hair; three types adhere to the head; one type adheres to the brain;
two types adhere to the mid-brain; three types are located on the forehead; two types adhere to the eye-roots; two types adhere to the ears;
two types adhere to the ear-roots; two types adhere to the nose-roots; two types adhere to the mouth-opening; and two types are located in the teeth.
Two types are located at the roots of the teeth; one type is on the tongue; one type adheres to the root of the tongue;
one type adheres to the upper palate in the mouth; one type is in the throat; two types are below the knees; two types adhere to the armpits;
two types are on the hands; one type adheres to the elbows; and two types are on the spleen; one type...
Regarding the attachments of the mind: one type attaches to the root of the breasts; one type attaches to the root of the spine; two types attach to the ribs; two types attach to the back;
one type attaches to the root of the navel; one type attaches to the skin; two types attach to the flesh;
four types attach to the bones; five types attach to the marrow; and two types attach to the large intestines. Two types attach to...
The small intestine: one part is in a warm place, one part is in a cold place, one part is in the path of excrement,
three parts are at the root of the large intestine, two parts adhere to the root of the hips, five parts adhere to the root of the genitals,
one part adheres to the joints of the fingers, one part is in the shins, and one part is at the kneecaps.
They are planted in the soles of the feet.

Thus, eighty kinds of worms inhabit the body, consuming it day and night; consequently, one hundred and one types of cold, heat, and wind diseases arise within the body, along with another one hundred and one miscellaneous illnesses. In this way, four hundred and four diseases are present within the body.

Just as fire produced from wood returns to burn that very wood, so too illness arises from the body; in this way, it merely destroys the body without distinction. Thus, internal destruction and illness likewise exist within; do not further inquire about external afflictions, for these constant destructive afflictions ruin this present life.
The present body is constantly clothed in decay; yet worldly people who do not hear this falsely imagine it to be solid, for they fail to see it with sincerity.

Hair, fur, nails, teeth, heart, flesh, skin, bones, clear blood, heat and affliction, the raw and the cooked, mucus, saliva, feces, and urine flow from the body—these are impermanent and impure, yet the deluded person imagines them to be pure.
The *duluer* (a type of acrobat or contortionist) peels his flesh and cuts it together, wrapping it around his body like a jujube fruit; such is the flesh of these "sour jujubes.

As for the fools who do not hear [the truth], the people of the world may attain physical composure, yet they ruin themselves and fall into affliction. They are like fish that see only the bait but do not see the hook or the net;
or again, like small children licking honey from a sharp blade, who crave only the sweetness and fail to see the edge of the knife.
Furthermore, it is like selling copper coated with gold leaf to deceive others; a foolish person, failing to perceive this, thinks it is pure gold and buys it, thereby bringing harm upon himself.
In the same way, people in the world may see those whose bodies are covered in skin as thin as jujube seeds, yet they do not realize that from such beings they will receive manifold afflictions.

When the skin of the jujube has thus peeled away, leaving only flesh, bone, and blood, people will tread upon it with their feet; constantly loathsome, they dare not even look at it—how could anyone dare to embrace it?
"When the retribution for one's past conduct— both calamities and blessings— is exhausted, or sometimes when life is cut short by an untimely death,
it is like a potter making vessels: some remain in the kiln,
while others emerge from the mold."
Whether it be while being processed in the wheel,
already processed,
or while being conveyed through the main stream, when it enters the furnace and is burned by fire;
Or when it has matured and is about to emerge;
or at the time of being consumed—it must inevitably perish.
The human body is also like this: whether it has fallen from the womb into the belly;
Either departing before the sense faculties have been formed;
or departing while the sense faculties are incomplete;
or departing at the time of birth.
Some depart as soon as they are born; some depart while still engaged in their studies;
some depart at sixteen, thirty, eighty, or a hundred years of age;
or after a period longer than that—yet inevitably, one must die.
The aggregates (skandhas) are thus fixed for no long time; as soon as they arise, they perish—perishing when the foot is lifted, perishing when the foot is set down.

Worldly people who have not heard [the Dharma] recklessly imagine themselves during childhood, youth, and old age, regarding the body as "this is my body," which differs from the intention of those who practice the Way.

The practitioner of the Path follows this principle: "Where there is existence, there is this; where there is non-existence, there is no such thing. What is meant by "where there is existence, there is this"?

From the commission of unwholesome deeds, there is death; from that death, consciousness falls into a state of attenuated karma; from attenuation, it becomes condensed; from condensation, the six sense-faculties gradually solidify; from the six sense-faculties, birth occurs; from birth, the body of an infant arises; from the infant's body, it grows into youth and adulthood; from youth and adulthood, one obtains the body subject to old age, sickness, and death—thus it constantly follows along.
In this way, the wheel of the world turns without interruption—unattached, empty, and like an illusion—ceaselessly pursuing its course;
it is like a fire breaking out in a city, fanned by the wind, as house after house burns together: the fire in the first house is not the fire in the second house, yet it is no different either.
It is simply that when the upper house has already burned, the next house burns as well, and thus it spreads by succession.
Birth and death are also like this: when these causes and conditions do not exist, that [result] also does not exist; when these cease, that also ceases.
"What is meant by 'neither being this nor being that'?
Since there is no death for one who has fundamentally practiced neither calamity nor merit, there is also nothing in the interim.
Since there is already no intermediate state, how could one possibly go anywhere?"
Since one cannot go [to birth], how could one be born?
Since one cannot be born, how could one undergo old age, sickness, and death?
Birth and death are like a flowing stream; if one does not perform the karma of birth and death, they will cease.
The practitioner of the Way should know that these five aggregates fundamentally arise from birth and extinction.
This constitutes the fifth stage of the Path, titled "The Chapter on Formation and Destruction. Chapter Six: The Practice of the Supernormal Powers (*ṛddhipāda*).

In the *Dàodì Jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Path), Chapter Six: The Practice of the Supernormal Powers. When wisdom enters the mind with clarity, it destroys evil as water breaks [through obstacles], and it causes flowers to bloom by departing from the seeds of the tree. It is a mass of merit that transcends worldly pleasures; it is like a refreshing breeze, delightful and beyond reproach. If one takes refuge in the single mind, where else could it be?

Without ceasing his intention to contemplate, as if being pulled by a hook on a scale, he heard the sutra that explains the cessation of contemplation regarding the world. Then, with palms joined and head bowed, he paid homage from all three realms.
At times, the practitioner first attains stillness (śamatha) and subsequently attains insight (vipaśyanā);
at other times, the practitioner is destined to attain insight first and subsequently attain stillness.
If the practitioner has already attained stillness of mind, they should seek liberation through insight.
If a practitioner has completed their contemplation, they should attain liberation through *śamatha*.
What are the characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
If the mind is focused on a single causal condition such that it rests in stillness and does not waver, nor does it stray to other thoughts, this is the characteristic of *śamatha*.

If one is in a state of stillness (*śamatha*), yet discriminates excessively or wanders off, one should contemplate according to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as follows: "There is feeling; this is the characteristic that should be contemplated.

It is like a gold merchant who, upon seeing gold, does not examine it by testing it. In this way, one should abide in stillness; yet if one takes up the gold and tests it to know whether it is gold, or whether it is mixed with copper from such-and-such a country or place and is not genuine, and knows the quality of the stone's color, its length or shortness, its roundness or squareness, its softness, or other defects—the contemplation is analogous to this.
It is, for example, like a person mowing grass: with the left hand he grasps the grass, and with the right hand holding a sickle, he cuts the grass.
In that analogy, grasping the grass is what should be stilled; cutting the grass is what should be contemplated.

For example, when a practitioner observes a skull and examines it with mature discernment, whether seeing it with eyes open or with eyes closed, the perception is identical and without difference; this is what should be stilled.

If one analytically contemplates that the skull bone is distinct, the jawbone is distinct, the teeth-bone is distinct, the neck-bone is distinct, and the bones of the arms, hands, ribs, throat, knees, and feet are each distinct—thus contemplating and thus seeing that the skeletal chain exists as a result of four causes and conditions.
What are the four? They are:

food, veneration, the union of practice, and the contemplation of bones; one should contemplate them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; as arising from impurity, as nothingness, and as that which should be observed.
To listen, one must not differentiate between the characteristics of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight);
this is *śamatha*. Differentiation is *vipaśyanā*.
What kind of practice does a practitioner maintain to attain the state of *śamatha*?
Response:
There are several causes for the cessation of mental activity.
Listen as I explain that there are two causal conditions through skillful means by which one attains the cessation of mental activity:
The first is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); the second is the mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breathing).
What is the practice of contemplating impurity?

Here, the practitioner directs his mind toward all people, wishing for their peace and well-being, and then proceeds to the "Father Tree" (*pitṛ-vṛkṣa*) to contemplate corpses. He contemplates those dead for one day up to seven days: the bloated, the livid-blue, the festering, the half-decomposed, the flesh-devoured, the blood-stained, the skeletal with bones still connected, the sinews still entwined, or those that are white and scattered in all directions, their hands and feet broken apart, resembling the color of a pigeon.

That practitioner takes one object at will and applies his mind so as to know it; before long, his mind becomes settled upon that object. He causes his mind to dwell upon the place where the object is spread out and observes it with mature and thorough discernment. If he knows for himself, "This is now the place where the object is spread out," he sees it clearly within that space; even when it is seen from a distance, it is likewise so.
In this state of emptiness, he sits upright in one place and sees; just as he saw when the causal conditions were laid out upon the ground, it is likewise according to those circumstances.

He then proceeds to a place free from sound and free from speech, sitting upright in a solitary, empty place, and sees as he did during his long-term practice, ensuring that his vision and mindfulness remain without variation.

If the practitioner, due to the conditions of the mental application (*manasikāra*), loses it and it is not received, and the mindfulness does not arise, they should again go to the tree of their father, causing the mind to receive the signs of the conditions of the mental application and causing the mind to sit; thus, they are led without departing, and mindfulness is always present before them.

If the practitioner’s mind, regarding the conditions of the mental application, enters and exits, travels far, yet remains constantly within the stationing of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) without being separated from it, keeping it in mind day and night, then for half a month, one month, or one year, they shall cause the practice not to be lost.

Whether walking, standing, sitting alone, or sitting among a great multitude; whether suffering from illness and fatigue or possessing physical strength—at all times, one should continuously follow [the practice] by keeping the causal conditions for the cultivation of the mind present before oneself. One should cultivate mindfulness of these causal conditions, reflecting that they are thus impermanent, empty, non-self, impure, and non-existent. One should cause the mental application based on these original causal conditions to proceed, maintaining mindfulness without deviation.

If one’s mind is focused on the place where the body is spread out and attains mastery, one then takes that reflection as the basis for observing one's own body; if one sees a corpse, it is equal to one's own body, with no difference whatsoever.
Whether seeing a man, or a weak person, or one who is old, or strong, or young;
whether they are unattractive, or naked, or clothed, or adorned—or even if it is oneself—it is just as when the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are established.
If the mind is directed toward whatever object, that object is entirely without distinction; thus, one should attain the cessation of the mind by means of the mindfulness of impurity (*aśubha*).
At that time, the mind follows its course, mindfulness does not depart, and practice reaches fulfillment, just as a river flows into the ocean.
Chapter 55: The Fifty-five Contemplations, Chapter Seven of the *Dao Di Jing*. The practitioner of the Path should contemplate their own body through fifty-five causal conditions:
this body is like foam, incapable of being grasped;
this body is like the great ocean, never satiated and never satisfied with the five pleasures.
This body is like a great river, destined by daily progression to reach the ocean of death;
this body is like excrement, which the wise do not desire;
this body is like a sandcastle, quickly crumbling and dispersing.
This body is like a city destined for destruction, filled with many enemies;
this body is like a conjured city, belonging to no one and incapable of being grasped;
this body is like a framework of bones smeared with flesh and blood.
This body is like a dilapidated cart, bound together by tendons;
this body is like a domestic cat, a mass of greed, hatred, and delusion;
this body is like one lost in a desolate wilderness, perpetually bewildered and wandering astray.
This body is like a vessel of forgetfulness, constantly losing all wholesome thoughts;
this body is like a jujube tree, with its hundred and eight modes of craving;
this body is like a broken jar, constantly leaking.
This body is like a painted jar, filled within with the most foul impurities;
this body is like a clean latrine because of its nine apertures;
this body is like a mass of blood, for it is loathed by others.
This body is like an illusion, yet the deluded take it to be real;
this body is like scabies;
this body is like a phantom, for it is attached to suffering.
This body is like a house made of rotten grain, for it is destroyed by food and drink;
this body is like a great cavern, for it is the dwelling place of many worms;
this body is like a skeleton, for it is filled with sin and impurities that do not decay.
This body is like an unglazed vessel, for it quickly breaks;
this body is like a bag with two mouths, where the pure enters and the impure exits;
this body is like a soiled garment, which is but a covering for the skeleton.
This body is like a cart, constantly traveling toward the burial ground;
this body is like dew or mist, which does not endure for long;
this body is like an ulcer, leaking from above.
This body is like a blind man, for it does not know the truths;
this body is like a dwelling place, for it contains four hundred and four diseases;
this body is like a pit, for it is a collection of all manner of impurities.
This body is like a hole in the ground where venomous snakes congregate;
this body is like an empty fist, deceived by fools;
this body is like a cemetery, always to be feared and loathed.
This body is like a tiger and a lion dwelling together, where anger erupts suddenly;
this body is like one afflicted by a severe epilepsy, due to the activity of the eighty-eight fetters;
this body is like one constantly smeared [with filth], fearing death.
This body is like gold coated with copper, for it is covered by skin;
this body is like an empty village, for within it constantly dwell the six internal decays;
this body is like a hungry ghost, for it is constantly seeking food and drink.
This body is like a place of fear, constantly subject to old age, sickness, and death;
this body is like a decaying skull, perpetually clothed in impurities;
this body is like an enemy, always bringing about circumstances that encounter adverse conditions.
This body is like the bark of a *kadamba* tree; though there is nothing substantial within its core, the deluded mind considers it to be most essential.
This body is like a leather bag, carrying many fetuses within its small space.
This body is like a rotting sack, foul and putrid.
This body is like deep darkness, where the sixty-two doubts do not abide;
this body is like joy and envy, which one cannot avoid but must undergo;
this body is like a decaying wall, arising from the conditions of evil thoughts.
This body is like a soiled garment, containing evil within;
this body is like a vessel that is not stable, constantly clinging to external decay;
this body is like a dwelling without support, indifferent to all things whether loved, unloved, or loathsome.
This body is like something that cannot be approached, for it is constantly shattered by contact;
this body is like something that can have no protector, for from time to time it is afflicted by diseases that loathe all things;
this body is like something that has no refuge of its own, for when death arrives, one cannot escape it.
*Dao di jing* (Sutra on the Stages of the Path), one fascicle.
